answer: FINAL HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded, NLSY79 1979 cohort): The Black–non-Hispanic-white "advantage" in college-degree-track/completed schooling is NOT a low-SES Black advantage. Because the file contains no degree variable, education is measured only as "Highest grade completed, 1979" (ages 14–22; right-truncated); a strict BA proxy (≥16 years) is essentially unobservable (age-20+ cells: Black 2/296 Low, 0/97 Mid, 2/64 High vs NBNH 4/602, 5/952, 19/781), so inference rests on the college-track outcome (any college ≥13 years) and continuous years of schooling. Among respondents aged 20+ (near-final education; BLACK n=512, NBNH n=2,442) stratified by a family-of-origin SES composite (log family income 1979 + mother's & father's education) in pooled tertiles: the Black-minus-NBNH college-track completion gap is ≈0 at LOW SES (−0.2pp, 95% CI −5.6 to +5.3), is positive and statistically distinguishable only at MIDDLE SES (+10.6pp, 95% CI +0.5 to +20.7; bootstrap 0.7–21.7; Black n=97), and reverts to ≤0 at HIGH SES (−2.5pp, n.s., Black n=64). Continuous years of schooling show no Black advantage at any SES: the largest Black deficit is at LOW SES (avg marginal ≈ −1.02 years, interaction p<0.001–0.0004) with ≈parity at mid SES. Unconditionally, age-20+ Black college-track completion is 26.2% vs NBNH 33.1% (gap −7.0pp, CI −11.2 to −2.7); mean schooling 11.11 vs 12.27 (−1.16 yrs). Robustness: the mid-SES Black advantage survives mother-education-only SES (+17.4pp, CI 7.4–27.5), MICE-lite imputation (+8.5pp), and Hispanic-inclusive comparison (+10.8pp, CI 0.5–21.1), but it does NOT appear at low/high SES, in continuous years of schooling, under income-only SES (age-20+ low-SES Black deficit −12.4pp, CI −19.8 to −4.9), under within-race relative-SES tertiles (gap negative at all levels, −3.5/−4.6/−8.7pp), or in the 1989-savings-data-restricted subsample (gaps ≤0; net savings amounts 79.3% missing). Conditional on ASVAB academic performance, gaps flip positive at all SES levels, indicating that at equal measured ability Black respondents are on a college track more often — but this is a conditional, ability-matched comparison, not the unconditional completion-rate advantage asked about. CONCLUSION: the relationship between any Black completion advantage and SES is non-monotonic (hump-shaped), concentrating at middle SES and built on college-entry rather than BA-degree completion; the largest Black completion deficits are at LOW SES — i.e., no advantage at the bottom of the SES distribution, contrary to a low-SES "advantage" framing.

payload.hypothesis: The Black-non-Hispanic-white advantage in college-degree-track/completed education is NOT a low-SES Black advantage: among NLSY79 respondents aged 20+ (near-final education), the Black-minus-NBNH any-college (>=13 yrs) completion gap is ~0 at low SES (-0.2pp), positive and significant only at MIDDLE SES (+10.6pp, 95% CI 0.5-20.7pp), and ~<=0 at high SES (-2.5pp); continuous years of schooling show the LARGEST Black deficit at low SES (~-1.0 yr, p<0.001). The relationship between any Black completion advantage and SES is non-monotonic (hump-shaped, centered at mid SES) and reflects college-entry rather than BA-degree completion, which is essentially unobservable in this file (HG>=16 cells: Black 2/296, 0/97, 2/64; NBNH 4/602, 5/952, 19/781).
payload.workflow: Load data/nls_raw.csv (12,686x61). Clean: HG79 (95->missing), outcomes BA(>=16, descriptive) and any-college(>=13) and continuous HG79; cohort BLACK(1) vs NBNH(3); SES composite z = mean of standardized log(income1979+1), mother ed, father ed; pooled tertiles (cutoffs -0.211, 0.330); covariates age, sex. Analyses: stratified rates & Black-minus-NBNH gaps (Wald CI) per SES level, full and age>=20; logistic (any-college) and OLS (HG79) with Black*C(ses)+age+male, reporting AME gaps per SES and interaction p; bootstrap (B=1000) CI for age>=20 headline gaps. Robustness: SES single-indicator (income-only; mother-ed-only), within-race tertile cutoffs, MICE-lite (5 imputations of loginc/moth/fath, chained regression), Hispanic-inclusive comparison (Black vs all non-Black), ASVAB-avg (+rel class rank) covariates, 1989 savings-direction covariate & interaction, adult-wealth (1985/1996) alternative SES. Diagnostics: per-cell n reported throughout; missingness carried into write-up (income-1979 19.6%, wealth-1996 44.5%, savings amount 79.3%, rank-in-class 55.4%, etc.). All deterministic (seed 42); script analysis.py; output log analysis_output.txt.
